Note that setting `_security` replaces the whole object; merge it with existing members.

## Connection string

The server URL with optional basic-auth credentials. The database name goes in the task, not in the URL:

```text
http://cdc:change-me@couch.internal:5984
https://cdc:change-me@account.cloudant.com
```

## Task fields

| Field | Meaning |

| table | The CouchDB database to follow (the source uses database when table is empty). |

## How changes are applied

- Primary key. The document `_id`. CouchDB ids may contain characters Meilisearch does not allow in ids; they are escaped (see document ids).

- Schema. Inferred from a sample of 100 documents.

- Design documents (`_design/…`) are skipped everywhere. Attachment stubs (`_attachments`) are removed from documents; `_rev` is kept.

- Snapshot. `_all_docs` with `include_docs=true`, 1,000 documents per page.

- Changes are read with `feed=longpoll` (requests wait up to 30 seconds for changes), 1,000 changes per request. A change with `"deleted": true` deletes the document; other changes upsert the winning revision.

- Transient HTTP failures are retried inside the source up to 5 times in a row before the task's own retry takes over.

- CouchDB has no truncate. Deleting the database stops the task with a permanent error.

## Positions and resume

Positions are the feed's opaque update sequences, kept verbatim (`12-g1AAAA…` on CouchDB 2 and later, `12` on 1.x). Resuming from one continues with the following changes; CouchDB may replay a few, which is harmless. If the server rejects a stored sequence, the position is lost and the task resyncs.

## Troubleshooting

| Error | Fix |

| couchdb: authentication failed …; check the user and password in the dsn | Fix the credentials in the URL. |

| couchdb: the user may not read database "products" …; add it to the database _security members | Add the user to the database's _security members. |

| couchdb: database "products" not found … | Create the database or fix the task's table. |

| couchdb: invalid dsn …: want http(s)://user:password@host:5984 | Use an absolute http or https URL. |


---

URL: https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/source-sqlserver.html

# SQL Server

The SQL Server source reads the change tables of SQL Server's built-in change data capture (CDC). CDC must be enabled on the database and the table, and SQL Server Agent must run.

## Prerequisites

### Enable CDC

As a member of `sysadmin` (for the database) and `db_owner` (for the table):

```sql
USE shop;
EXEC sys.sp_cdc_enable_db;

EXEC sys.sp_cdc_enable_table
     @source_schema = N'dbo',
     @source_name   = N'products',
     @role_name     = NULL;
```

This creates the capture instance `dbo_products`, its change table `cdc.dbo_products_CT`, and the capture and cleanup jobs. With `@role_name = NULL` no gating role is required to read the changes; if you set a role, add the CDC user to it.

### SQL Server Agent

The Agent runs the capture job that fills the change tables. When the source can see that the Agent is stopped, the task fails with:

```text
sqlserver: SQL Server Agent is stopped, so the CDC capture job does not run; start it (Linux containers: MSSQL_AGENT_ENABLED=true)
```

In the official Linux container, set `MSSQL_AGENT_ENABLED=true`. The check reads `sys.dm_server_services`; it is skipped where that view does not exist (Azure SQL Database) or when the user lacks `VIEW SERVER STATE`.

### A dedicated user

```sql
USE shop;
CREATE LOGIN cdc WITH PASSWORD = 'Change-me-123';
CREATE USER cdc FOR LOGIN cdc;
GRANT SELECT ON dbo.products TO cdc;     -- snapshot
GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA::cdc TO cdc;      -- change tables and cdc.lsn_time_mapping
-- optional, lets the task detect a stopped Agent:
USE master; GRANT VIEW SERVER STATE TO cdc;
```

## Connection string

```text
sqlserver://cdc:Change-me-123@sql.internal:1433?database=shop
sqlserver://cdc:Change-me-123@sql.internal:1433?database=shop&encrypt=true&trustservercertificate=false
```

The database must be in the connection string (`?database=`) or in the task's `database`. Connected to `master`, `tempdb`, `model` or `msdb`, the task fails and asks for the database.

## Task fields

| Field | Default | Meaning |

| schema | dbo | Schema of the table. |

| table | required | The CDC-enabled table. |

| slot (API only) | {schema}_{table} | The capture instance to read. When the default does not exist, the newest capture instance of the table is used. Useful during a schema change, when a table has two capture instances. |

## How changes are applied

- Primary key required. The table needs a primary key, and the capture instance must capture every key column.

- Captured columns only. Only the columns captured by the capture instance are read. A column added to the table after the capture instance was created is not captured; create a new capture instance (and pass it as `slot`) to include it.

- Snapshot. Keyset pages of 5,000 rows.

- Changes are polled every 500 ms, up to 5,000 change rows at a time. This adds to the capture job's own latency, a few seconds by default. Inserts and updates upsert; deletes delete.

- Commit times come from `cdc.lsn_time_mapping`, which SQL Server records in server local time; they are reported as UTC, so lag is off by the server's UTC offset when the server does not run in UTC.

## Positions and resume

Positions are `lsnhex:seqvalhex`: the `__$start_lsn` and `__$seqval` of the last change row delivered, 20 lowercase hex digits each, for example `0000002b000004880021:0000002b000004880020`. The task resumes strictly after it.

The cleanup job removes change rows older than its retention period (3 days by default). A position older than the capture instance's minimum LSN is lost and the task resyncs automatically. A task that is idle (no changes) for longer than the retention also sees this, because its stored position stops moving while the low-water mark advances.

## Troubleshooting

| Error | Fix |

| change data capture is not enabled for database "shop"; as sysadmin run: USE [shop]; EXEC sys.sp_cdc_enable_db; | Run the printed statement. |

| table dbo.products is not tracked by change data capture; run: EXEC sys.sp_cdc_enable_table … | Run the printed statement. |

| read cdc.change_tables (the user needs SELECT on the cdc schema) | GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA::cdc TO cdc; |

| capture instance "dbo_products" no longer exists (CDC was disabled for the table?) | Enable CDC on the table again, then resync. |

| SQL Server Agent is stopped … | Start the Agent. |


---

URL: https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/source-cockroachdb.html

# CockroachDB

The CockroachDB source uses a core (sinkless) changefeed, which needs no enterprise license and no Kafka or cloud-storage sink. The snapshot is a consistent read at the changefeed's starting timestamp.

## Prerequisites

Changefeeds need rangefeeds. If `kv.rangefeed.enabled` is false, the task tries to enable it; when the user may not change cluster settings, the task fails and asks an admin to run:

```sql
SET CLUSTER SETTING kv.rangefeed.enabled = true;
```

The table needs an explicit primary key. A table that only has CockroachDB's hidden `rowid` is refused with a hint to run `ALTER TABLE … ALTER PRIMARY KEY USING COLUMNS (…)`.

### A dedicated user

```sql
CREATE USER cdc WITH PASSWORD 'change-me';
GRANT SELECT, CHANGEFEED ON TABLE shop.public.products TO cdc;
```

Missing privileges fail the task with `(the user needs SELECT and CHANGEFEED privileges on the table)`.

## Connection string

CockroachDB speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol; use a PostgreSQL URL with the database in the path:

```text
postgresql://cdc:change-me@crdb.internal:26257/shop?sslmode=verify-full
postgresql://root@localhost:26257/shop?sslmode=disable        # insecure local cluster
```

## Task fields

| Field | Default | Meaning |

| table | required | The table in the connection's database. |

| schema (API only) | public | Schema of the table. |

## How changes are applied

- Snapshot. Keyset pages of 5,000 rows read `AS OF SYSTEM TIME` the position captured before the copy, so the copy is consistent and the changefeed continues exactly from there.

- Stream. `CREATE CHANGEFEED FOR TABLE … WITH updated, resolved = '1s', format = json, cursor = '…'` (older versions fall back to `EXPERIMENTAL CHANGEFEED FOR`). Rows are read as JSON in both phases, so they carry identical values: numbers become integers or floats, `TIMESTAMP`/`TIMESTAMPTZ` become times, other values stay as CockroachDB renders them in JSON.

- Deletes arrive as rows with a null `after` image and delete the document.

- Truncates are not captured by changefeeds; resync the task after a `TRUNCATE`.

## Positions and resume

Positions are CockroachDB HLC timestamps in decimal form, for example `1700000000123456789.0000000001`. Changefeed rows are only ordered per key, so every event carries the latest resolved timestamp seen so far: everything at or before it has been delivered, and restarting from it replays at most a few changes.

A position older than the table's garbage collection window (`gc.ttlseconds`) cannot be resumed; the task resyncs automatically. Keep tasks running, or raise the TTL for tables whose tasks may be stopped for long.

## Troubleshooting

| Error | Fix |

| changefeeds need rangefeeds, but kv.rangefeed.enabled is false and this user cannot change it | Run SET CLUSTER SETTING kv.rangefeed.enabled = true as an admin. |

| table public.x has no primary key (it uses the hidden rowid column) | Add a primary key. |

| table public.x does not exist in the current database | Put the right database in the connection string. |


---

URL: https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/source-kafka.html

# Kafka (Debezium)

The Kafka source consumes [Debezium](https://debezium.io) change events from a topic. Anything Debezium captures (Oracle, Db2, Cassandra, Informix, Vitess, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL…) can feed Meilisearch this way.

## Prerequisites

- A Debezium connector writing one table's changes to one topic, typically `..`.

- The JSON converter for keys and values, with or without schemas. Avro and Protobuf are not supported.

- Brokers reachable from the service in plaintext: the connector takes a list of `host:port` brokers and has no SASL or TLS settings.

```json
{
  "name": "inventory-connector",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
    "topic.prefix": "dbserver1",
    "table.include.list": "inventory.customers",
    "key.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.json.JsonConverter",
    "value.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.json.JsonConverter",
    "key.converter.schemas.enable": "true",
    "value.converter.schemas.enable": "true"
  }
}
```

(Database connection settings of the Debezium connector are omitted; see the Debezium documentation for your database.)

## Connection settings

| Field | Meaning |

| brokers | One or more host:port seed brokers, for example kafka-1:9092, kafka-2:9092. |

## Task fields

| Field | Default | Meaning |

| table | required | The Debezium topic, for example dbserver1.inventory.customers. A missing topic fails with a hint to check topic.prefix and the table include list. |

| groupId | cdc- | The consumer group whose committed offsets track progress. Never share it with other consumers. |

## How changes are applied

- Envelope. Messages may be wrapped as `{"schema": …, "payload": …}` or be the bare envelope. Debezium's `op` is mapped: `c`, `u` and `r` (snapshot read) upsert the `after` image; `d` deletes using the `before` image, or the message key when there is none; `t` is a truncate. Tombstones (empty values after a delete), heartbeats, schema changes and transaction metadata are skipped.

- Types. With schemas enabled, Debezium logical types are converted: `io.debezium.time.Timestamp`, `MicroTimestamp`, `NanoTimestamp`, `ZonedTimestamp`, `Date` and Kafka Connect `Timestamp`/`Date` become times; `org.apache.kafka.connect.data.Decimal` becomes a number.

- Schema and key. Columns are inferred from up to 50 messages read in at most 5 seconds from the start of the topic. The primary key comes from the message key's fields (`id` when it cannot be determined); set `mapping.primaryKey` to override it.

- Snapshot. Replays the topic from its start up to the current end offsets and keeps the latest image per message key in memory, then writes the rows still alive. Memory grows with the number of live rows.

Very large topics

Use the `stream` sync mode instead of `snapshot_stream`: the topic is consumed from the group's committed offsets, or from the earliest offset when the group has none, as ordinary change events, without holding the table in memory. Debezium's own snapshot (`op: r`) then fills the index.

## Positions and resume

A position is a JSON object mapping `topic/partition` to the next offset to read. Confirmed positions are also committed to the consumer group, so tools like `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group cdc-<task>` show the task's lag. If an offset is no longer available (topic retention removed it), the position is lost and the task resyncs automatically.

## Troubleshooting

| Error | Fix |

| kafka: topic "…" does not exist; check the Debezium connector topic.prefix and table include list | Use the exact topic name Debezium writes. |

| kafka: delete without before image or key | Keep the message key (do not drop it in an SMT), or enable before images on the source. |

| Decoding errors on every message | The topic uses Avro or Protobuf; switch the connector to the JSON converter. |


---

URL: https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/source-redis.html

# Redis Streams

The Redis source reads a Redis stream that your application appends changes to with `XADD`. Use it when your code already knows what changed and Redis sits next to it.

## Entry format

Append one entry per change. Fields:

| Field | Meaning |

| op | upsert (default; insert, update and replace are aliases), delete or truncate. Any other value stops the task with entry … has unknown op. |

| id | The document key. It is copied into the row as id unless the row already has an id. |

| data | Optional JSON object with the whole row. Without data, every other field except op becomes a column, as a string (Redis field values are strings). |

```bash
XADD items * op upsert id 42 data '{"name":"shoe","price":9.5,"tags":["sale"]}'
XADD items * id 42 name shoe price 9.5          # same row, values as strings
XADD items * op delete id 42
XADD items * op truncate                          # holds the task unless allowTruncate
```

Prefer `data` with JSON when you need numbers, booleans or nested values in Meilisearch (for filters and sorting).

## Connection string

```text
redis://:password@redis.internal:6379/0
redis://cdc:password@redis.internal:6379/0      # Redis 6+ ACL user
rediss://cdc:password@redis.internal:6380/0     # TLS
```

The user needs to read the stream: with ACLs, for example `ACL SETUSER cdc on >password ~items +ping +type +xrange +xrevrange +xread +xinfo|stream +scan` (`SCAN` is only used by the connector's stream browser). The key must be a stream or not exist yet; any other type fails with `key "items" is a hash, not a stream`.

## Task fields

| Field | Meaning |

| table | The stream key, for example items. |

The primary key is always `id`. The schema shown in the wizard is inferred from a sample of entries.

## How it works

- Snapshot. A stream is a log, not a table: the snapshot replays the whole stream from the beginning, keeps the latest image per key (like a compacted log) and writes the rows still alive at the end. That image is held in memory.

- Stream. `XREAD` without a consumer group, 1,000 entries at a time, blocking at most 500 ms per call. The task's `groupId` is ignored, nothing is acknowledged in Redis, and the service never trims the stream. Trim it yourself (`XADD … MAXLEN ~ …` or `XTRIM`) with a margin that covers task downtime.

## Positions and resume

Positions are stream entry ids such as `1700000000000-0`; `0-0` is the start. On resume the source checks that nothing after the position was trimmed or deleted, and that the stream was not recreated (a position after the last generated id). Otherwise the position is lost and the task resyncs. The precise checks use fields of `XINFO STREAM` added in Redis 7.


---

URL: https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/source-sqlpoll.html

# SQL polling

When log-based capture is not available (no replication privileges, a managed database that hides its log, SQLite), the `sqlpoll` source re-reads a table on an interval and picks up rows whose cursor column moved forward.

## Requirements

- A driver: `pgx` (PostgreSQL; `postgres` and `postgresql` are aliases), `mysql` (MySQL and MariaDB; alias `mariadb`) or `sqlite` (alias `sqlite3`).

- A primary key, used to page through rows: `table … has no primary key; sqlpoll needs one to page through rows` otherwise.

- A cursor column that grows with every insert and update: an `updated_at` timestamp maintained by the application or a trigger, or a version number bumped on every write.

- `SELECT` on the table. No other privilege is needed.

Example for PostgreSQL, keeping `updated_at` current with a trigger:

```sql
ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN updated_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now();
CREATE INDEX ON products (updated_at, id);

CREATE FUNCTION touch_updated_at() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN NEW.updated_at := clock_timestamp(); RETURN NEW; END $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;
CREATE TRIGGER products_touch BEFORE UPDATE ON products
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION touch_updated_at();
```

For MySQL: `updated_at TIMESTAMP(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6) ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6)`. An index on the cursor column (followed by the key) keeps each poll cheap.

## Connection settings

| Driver | DSN example |

| pgx | postgres://reader:secret@db.internal:5432/shop |

| mysql | reader:secret@tcp(db.internal:3306)/shop (parseTime is enabled automatically) |

| sqlite | file:/var/data/app.sqlite |

## Task fields

| Field | Default | Meaning |

| table | required | The table to poll. |

| schema (API only) | driver default | Schema of the table. |

| cursorColumn | required | The column that grows with every write. The wizard ranks candidates (updated_at, modified_at, last_modified, changed_at, version, row_version, rowversion, then timestamps and integers). |

| pollInterval | 2s | How often to look for changes. The wizard offers 500 ms to 1 minute; any duration works through the API. |

## How it works

- Snapshot. Keyset pages of 1,000 rows by primary key.

- Polling. Every interval, the source reads rows whose `(cursor, primary key)` is greater than the last one delivered, 1,000 at a time, and keeps reading until a page comes back short. Each row becomes an upsert.

- Deletes need soft deletes. A hard `DELETE` is invisible: the row simply stops being returned. Mark rows deleted instead (a `deleted` flag or a `deleted_at` column that also bumps the cursor) and set the task's soft delete column, so those rows delete their documents.

## Limitations

- Rows whose cursor is `NULL` are never streamed (the snapshot still copies them).

- A write that commits with a cursor lower than one already polled is missed: for example a long transaction that stamped `updated_at` at its start, or sequence values allocated out of order. Prefer a cursor assigned at commit time, or keep transactions short compared with the poll interval. A periodic diff and repair catches anything missed.

- On SQLite prefer an integer cursor: time values are bound as text and compare lexically against however the column was written.

- No truncate detection.

## Positions and resume

A position is JSON with the cursor and primary key of the last row delivered, for example `{"cursor":"2026-10-26T10:00:00.123456Z","pk":[42]}`. A null cursor means "from the beginning" (the table was empty when the position was taken). A position that cannot be decoded is treated as lost and the task resyncs.


---

URL: https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/source-webhook.html

# Webhook (HTTP push)

A webhook task has no database to read: your application POSTs its changes to `/api/v1/ingest/{task id}`, and the request returns once the documents are confirmed in Meilisearch.

## Create the task

- Create a connector of type Webhook. It has no connection settings.

- Create a task on it. The table is only a name for the feed (it appears in logs). Set a primary key column in the mapping step if your rows do not have an `id` field.

- Optionally add a signing secret (see signed requests). Generate creates a random `whsec_…` value; copy it then, because it is never shown again.

- Start the task. Its Overview tab shows a Push endpoint card with the URL and, for signed tasks, a ready-to-run signed `curl` example.

The task id is in the URL, so give the task a readable id (for example `products-push`) when you create it.

## Payload

The body is a single change, a JSON array of changes, or newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON), up to 64 MiB:

```json
{"op": "upsert", "row": {"id": 1, "name": "Desk lamp", "price": 39.9}}
```

```json
[
  {"op": "upsert", "row": {"id": 1, "name": "Desk lamp"}},
  {"op": "delete", "row": {"id": 2}},
  {"row": {"id": 3, "name": "Chair"}}
]
```

```text
{"op":"upsert","row":{"id":4,"name":"Shelf"}}
{"op":"delete","row":{"id":5}}
```

| Field | Meaning |

| op | upsert (default; insert, update and replace are aliases), delete or truncate. |

| row | The row as a JSON object. Required and non-empty for upserts and deletes; a delete needs at least the key columns. Integral numbers become integers, others floats. |

Changes in one request are applied in order, and requests to one task are applied in the order they arrive. A `truncate` holds the task unless `allowTruncate` is on.

## Responses

| Status | Meaning |

| 200 {"accepted":n,"position":"…"} | Every change is durably in Meilisearch. |

| 400 | Invalid payload (the error says why), or the task is not a webhook task. |

| 401 | Not authenticated, or the signature is missing, wrong, or stale. |

| 403 | Authenticated, but the role is below moderator. |

| 503 | the task is not running; start it and retry. |

| 504 | changes were not confirmed in time; retry (writes are idempotent) after 60 seconds. |

Retry on `503`, `504` and network errors: the same change applied twice gives the same document.

## Authentication

How a push authenticates depends on whether the task has a signing secret (`source.webhookSecret`):

| Task | What the request needs |

| No secret | A bearer token or session with at least the moderator role. The static CDC_ADMIN_TOKEN works: Authorization: Bearer …. |

| Secret set | A valid signature. No token is needed, and a token alone is refused with 401. |

Anonymous callers get `401` both for unknown task ids and for tasks without a secret, so task ids cannot be probed.

```bash
# Task without a secret: a token with the moderator role or higher
curl -X POST "https://cdc.example.com/api/v1/ingest/products-push" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CDC_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"op":"upsert","row":{"id":1,"name":"Desk lamp"}}'
```

## Signed requests

With a signing secret (at least 16 characters), each request carries two headers:

```text
X-CDC-Timestamp: 1767225600
X-CDC-Signature: sha256=<hex HMAC-SHA256(secret, timestamp + "." + raw body)>
```

The timestamp is in Unix seconds and must be within 5 minutes of the server clock. The HMAC covers the timestamp, a dot, and the exact bytes of the body, so sign what you send. A request is refused with `401` when it is unsigned (`the request is not signed: send the X-CDC-Timestamp and X-CDC-Signature headers`), signed with another secret or over a changed body (`the signature does not match …`), or too old or too far in the future (`the signature timestamp is outside the accepted 5 minute window; check the sender's clock`).

### With curl and openssl

```bash
CDC=https://cdc.example.com
TASK=products-push
SECRET='whsec_…'                       # the task's signing secret
BODY='{"op":"upsert","row":{"id":1,"name":"Desk lamp"}}'
TS=$(date +%s)
SIG=$(printf '%s.%s' "$TS" "$BODY" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$SECRET" | sed 's/^.* //')
curl -X POST "$CDC/api/v1/ingest/$TASK" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H "X-CDC-Timestamp: $TS" -H "X-CDC-Signature: sha256=$SIG" -d "$BODY"
```

### From Node.js

```javascript
import { createHmac } from 'node:crypto';

async function push(changes) {
  const body = JSON.stringify(changes);
  const ts = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000).toString();
  const sig = createHmac('sha256', process.env.CDC_WEBHOOK_SECRET).update(`${ts}.${body}`).digest('hex');
  const res = await fetch('https://cdc.example.com/api/v1/ingest/products-push', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'X-CDC-Timestamp': ts, 'X-CDC-Signature': `sha256=${sig}` },
    body,
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${res.status} ${await res.text()}`);
  return res.json(); // {accepted, position}
}
```

### Rotating the secret

The secret is encrypted at rest and returned masked (`••••••`). In the task's Edit page, Rotate generates a new one and Remove clears it (the API takes `""` to remove it; sending the mask back keeps the stored one). The `X-CDC-Signature` header may hold several comma-separated signatures, and any one that matches is accepted, so a sender can sign with both the old and the new secret while you switch.

## Positions and limits

Positions are a per-task sequence number (`0`, `1`, `2`…), one per pushed change. Pushes are queued in memory (64 requests wait at most; further pushers block) and are not kept across restarts: a push that was not confirmed when the service stopped fails, and the sender must retry. The schema is a single `id` column (the primary key unless the mapping names another).

Do not resync a webhook task

The webhook source has nothing to copy: its snapshot is empty. A Resync (or a Reset checkpoint while zero-downtime resync is on) rebuilds the index from nothing: an in-place resync clears it, and a zero-downtime rebuild swaps in an empty shadow index. Your application then has to push every document again. Use the `stream` sync mode for webhook tasks: it refuses resyncs (`409`, `resync needs a snapshot`). Never use `snapshot` mode.


---

URL: https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/destinations.html

# Meilisearch destinations

A destination is a named Meilisearch instance that tasks write to. Add as many as you need (regions, staging, a search replica) and fan one table out to several of them with several tasks.

Destinations with live health, version, documents and the tasks writing to each.

## Add a destination

Go to Destinations → Add destination (admin role). Test checks the URL and key before saving and reports the version, latency and number of indexes.

| Field | Default | Meaning |

| Name | required | A label shown everywhere, for example Production (EU). |

| URL | required | Absolute http or https URL of the instance, for example https://ms-1234.meilisearch.io. A trailing slash is removed. |

| API key | empty | The key sent as a bearer token. Stored encrypted, shown as ••••••; keep the mask to keep the stored key. |

| Gzip requests | on in the dashboard | Compress request bodies. Saves bandwidth to remote instances; turn it off on loopback or a LAN to save CPU. In the API the JSON field gzip is false when omitted. |

| Timeout | 30s | Per-request timeout. |

| Health check every | 30s | Background check interval, between 5s and 1h. The dashboard offers 5 s to 10 minutes; the API accepts any value in range. |

| Tags, description | empty | For your own organisation. |

The first destination becomes the default: tasks that do not name a destination write there, and index pages open on it. Make default moves the flag. A task's empty `index.destinationId` is resolved to the default when the task is saved, so later changing the default does not move existing tasks.

## API key permissions

The simplest choice is the instance's master key or its Default Admin API Key. If you create a dedicated key, include the actions the features you use need. These follow from the Meilisearch API calls the service makes:

| Feature | Meilisearch actions |

| Syncing (snapshot and stream) | documents.add, documents.delete, indexes.create, indexes.get, indexes.update (primary key of an empty index), stats.get, tasks.get |

| Managed index settings | settings.get, settings.update |

| Zero-downtime resync | indexes.create, indexes.swap, indexes.delete, settings.get, settings.update, tasks.get; plus dumps.create with dump before resync |

| Health checks | version, stats.get (the /health route needs no key) |

| Dashboard: search, documents, diff | search, documents.get |

| Dashboard: task queue, backups | tasks.get, tasks.cancel, dumps.create, snapshots.create |

| Dashboard: index admin | indexes.delete, indexes.swap, settings.update, and the compaction action of your Meilisearch version |

Scope the key's `indexes` to the index uids your tasks use, plus `*__cdc_shadow_*` if you enable zero-downtime resync (shadow indexes are named `<uid>__cdc_shadow_<unix time>`). Experimental features use Meilisearch's `/experimental-features` route, which may need the master key. A rejected key stops tasks with a configuration error (`invalid_api_key`), rather than retrying.

## Health

Every destination is checked in the background at its interval. A check reads the version, the number of indexes and documents and the database size, and records the latency. The destination page and list show:

- healthy or unreachable, with the last error and the number of consecutive failures;

- version, indexes, documents, database size, latency, the last time it was healthy and the next check;

- the tasks writing to it with their state, index, lag, rate and last sync, and an aggregate (tasks, running, failing, last sync, maximum lag, rate).

Each completed check is pushed live to dashboards (`destination.health` events). Check now runs one immediately (moderator). Testing a destination's connection needs admin. An alert rule of type `meili_down` notifies you when an instance stays unreachable; see [Alerts](https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/alerts.html).

## Edit and delete

- Changing the URL or the API key restarts the running tasks that write to the destination. A new interval takes effect at once.

- A destination used by tasks cannot be deleted (`409` with the tasks), and the default destination cannot be deleted; make another one the default first.

## Per-instance pages

Each destination has its own page with tabs:

The detail page of one Meilisearch instance.

| Tab | What it shows |

| Overview | Health, statistics and the tasks writing here. |

| Indexes | The instance's indexes with document counts and the tasks that manage them. See Index management. |

| Meilisearch tasks | The instance's task queue, filterable by index, status and type; enqueued tasks can be cancelled (moderator). Writes made by meilisearch-cdc carry the custom metadata cdc:. |

| Backups | Request a dump or a snapshot of the instance (admin). Meilisearch writes them to its own dump and snapshot directories. |

| Experimental | Meilisearch's experimental features as toggles (admin; read only for others). |

| Settings | The destination's own fields (name, URL, key, gzip, timeout, interval). |

The top-level Indexes and Meilisearch tasks pages show the same information for every instance at once, grouped per instance.

## Single-instance mode

When `MEILI_URL` is set, the service writes only to that instance. It appears as destination `default`, marked managed by env, with its URL and key read only, and adding, deleting or switching destinations is refused with `409`. See [Configuration](https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/configuration.html#single-instance-mode).


---

URL: https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/tasks.html

# Create a task

A task connects one source table to one Meilisearch index. The wizard walks through six steps; every option it shows maps to a field of the task JSON used by the API and the tasks file.

Open Tasks → New task (admin role). The steps are Connector, Source, Mapping, Index, Sync & safety and Review. Errors are shown on the step they belong to, and the review lists anything left to fix.

## 1. Connector

Pick the saved connector to read from, or add one from the side panel without leaving the wizard. Credentials live in the connector only; the task never repeats them. See [Connectors](https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/sources.html#connectors).

Step 1: choose a connector.

## 2. Source

Basics, then what to sync:

| Field | JSON | Notes |

| Name | name | Required. |

| Task id | id | Optional. Letters, digits, - and _, at most 64 characters. The wizard derives it from the name when empty; the API generates a random one. It cannot change later and names the replication slot, consumer group and webhook URL. |

| Description, tags | description, tags | Tags filter the task list. |

| Table (or collection, topic, stream…) | source.table | Required. Pick from the tables the connector lists, or type it. |

| Source-specific fields | source.schema, source.database, source.slot, source.publication, source.serverId, source.groupId, source.cursorColumn, source.pollInterval, source.webhookSecret | Shown only for the sources that use them; each source page explains them. |

Test connection (moderator) connects through the connector, reads the table's schema and transforms five sample rows with the current mapping, so you see real documents before anything is written. It uses `POST /api/v1/tasks/test`. For PostgreSQL, testing also creates the task's publication if it does not exist yet.

## 3. Mapping

The mapping turns rows into documents.

Step 3: document identity, fields, transforms and static fields.

### Document identity

| Field | JSON | Default | Meaning |

| Primary key columns | mapping.primaryKey | the source's primary key | Source columns that identify a row. Several columns build a composite id. Required when the source has no primary key. |

| Primary key field | mapping.primaryKeyField | id | The document field that holds the id; it becomes the index's primary key. |

| Keep key columns | mapping.keepKeyColumns | off | Also copy the original key columns into the document. Off: a key column is left out, unless it is the single key column and has the same name as the primary key field. |

#### How document ids are built

- A single integer key is written as a number (`42`).

- Other single keys are written as strings. Values made only of `a-z A-Z 0-9 -` (integers, UUIDs, slugs) are kept as they are. Anything else is escaped into Meilisearch's id alphabet: `_` becomes `__` and every other byte becomes `_XX` (hex). For example `user@example.com` becomes `user_40example_2Ecom`. Escaped ids always contain `_` and raw ones never do, so two different keys never collide.

- Composite keys join their escaped parts with `-` (a `-` inside a part is escaped too): `(7, "fr")` becomes `7-fr`.

- Ids longer than 511 bytes are replaced by `h-` and a SHA-256 hex digest.

- A row without a value for a key column cannot become a document; it goes to the dead letter queue as a `transform` entry and the checkpoint moves on.

Two tasks may write to the same index (with the `upsert` write mode, to merge fields from several tables), but only with the same primary key field: saving a task whose key field differs from another task on that index and destination fails with `409`.

### Fields

| Field | JSON | Meaning |

| Include | mapping.include | Copy only these columns (key columns are always available for the id). Empty copies every column. |

| Exclude | mapping.exclude | Drop these columns. Applied after include. |

| Rename | mapping.rename | Map of source column to document field, for example {"customer_email": "email"}. |

### Transforms

| Field | JSON | Meaning |

| Soft delete column and value | mapping.softDeleteColumn, mapping.softDeleteValue | Rows whose column matches turn into deletes. With an empty value, any non-null value deletes (a deleted_at timestamp, say), except boolean false. With a value, the column's text is compared case-insensitively, for example true or 1. |

| Geo latitude and longitude columns | mapping.geo.lat, mapping.geo.lng | Build Meilisearch's _geo field {"lat": …, "lng": …} from two numeric (or numeric string) columns. When either is missing or not a number, _geo is written as null. Add _geo to the filterable and sortable attributes to use geosearch. The source columns themselves are still copied unless excluded. |

| Time format | mapping.timeFormat | rfc3339 (default; ISO 8601 strings in UTC, readable but not usable for range filters or chronological sorting), unix (seconds since the epoch: filterable and sortable numbers) or unix_ms (milliseconds). |

### Static fields

`mapping.static` adds the same fields to every document, for example `{"tenant": "acme", "source": "eu-db"}`. This is handy for multi-tenant indexes fed by several tasks. Static fields overwrite source columns of the same name; the primary key field always wins.

## 4. Index

Step 4: destination, index uid, write mode and managed settings.

| Field | JSON | Default | Meaning |

| Destination | index.destinationId | the default destination | The Meilisearch instance to write to. |

| Index uid | index.uid | the table name | Required; a-z A-Z 0-9 - _, up to 400 characters. Created on first write when missing, with the primary key field as its primary key. The wizard suggests existing indexes and shows their document count and other writers. |

| Write mode | index.writeMode | replace | replace sends whole documents (Meilisearch POST /documents): fields removed in the source disappear. upsert merges fields into existing documents (PUT /documents): useful when several tasks write one index, or when the source omits unchanged columns (PostgreSQL TOAST). In upsert mode a document deleted and re-created in the same batch is replaced, so stale fields do not come back. |

| Manage index settings | index.manageSettings | off | Apply index.settings when the task starts (and when you save it while stopped), and report drift in the schema check. |

| Settings | index.settings | none | Meilisearch index settings, the same JSON as Meilisearch's PATCH /indexes/{uid}/settings. Only the keys you set are managed. Edited with the settings editor. Unknown keys are rejected. |

## 5. Sync & safety

### Sync mode

| Mode | JSON | Behaviour |

| Snapshot + stream | snapshot_stream (default) | Copy the existing rows, then stream every change. The usual choice. |

| Stream only | stream | Start from the current position; existing rows are not copied. Resync is refused in this mode. |

| Snapshot only | snapshot | Copy the rows once; the task then shows completed and stops. |

### Batching

| Field | JSON | Default | Meaning |

| Batch size | sync.batchSize | 1000 | Documents per Meilisearch request. Larger batches index faster and use more memory; 5,000 to 10,000 suits big snapshots. |

| Flush interval | sync.flushInterval | 1s | The longest a change waits in a partial batch. Lower it for lower latency on quiet tables. |

| Max in-flight | sync.maxInflight | 4 | Batches sent to Meilisearch and not yet confirmed. Meilisearch auto-batches consecutive tasks, so 8 helps bulk loads. |

Within a batch, changes to the same document are coalesced and only the final state is sent. Confirmations are processed in order, so checkpoints never skip an unconfirmed batch. See [Performance and tuning](https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/performance.html).

### Retry

| Field | JSON | Default | Meaning |

| Max attempts | sync.retry.maxAttempts | 8 | Attempts for one Meilisearch write before the pipeline gives up and restarts. |

| Initial backoff | sync.retry.initialBackoff | 200ms | First wait; waits grow exponentially with full jitter. |

| Max backoff | sync.retry.maxBackoff | 30s | Upper bound of a wait. |

Network errors, Meilisearch `5xx`, `429` and `408` are retried. A payload that is too large is split in half. Documents Meilisearch rejects are isolated into the dead letter queue. Configuration errors (a bad API key, an index whose primary key differs) stop the task as `failed`. When the attempts run out, the pipeline restarts with its own backoff (1 s up to 1 minute) and the task shows `retrying`.

### Safety guards

| Field | JSON | Wizard default | API default | Meaning |

| Max delete ratio | sync.safety.maxDeleteRatio | 0.2 (20%) | 0 (off) | Hold the task when one flush would delete more than this share of the index (0 to 1; 0 disables the guard). |

| Min docs for delete guard | sync.safety.minDocsForDeleteGuard | 1000 | 1000 | The ratio check is skipped while the index has fewer documents. |

| Allow TRUNCATE | sync.safety.allowTruncate | off | off | Let a source truncate (or a dropped MongoDB collection) delete every document. When off, the task is held. |

| Zero-downtime resync | sync.safety.zeroDowntimeResync | on | off | Rebuild into a shadow index and swap it in when complete, so search keeps working during a resync. |

| Dump before resync | sync.safety.dumpBeforeResync | off | off | Ask Meilisearch for a dump before a zero-downtime rebuild starts (best effort: a failed dump is logged, the rebuild continues). |

A held task has stopped before applying the risky batch, so nothing was lost and nothing was deleted. Look at the source, then Resume (the batch is retried, and holds again if the guard still applies), raise the guard, or Resync. The hold reason is in the task's status, for example `safety hold: a single batch would delete 5000 of 8000 documents (62% > 20% limit)` or `safety hold: the source table was truncated; enable safety.allowTruncate or resync the task`. The delete guard reads the index size at most every 10 seconds.

## 6. Review

The review summarises the task, shows its JSON and lists any field that needs attention. Create saves it stopped; Create & start starts it right away (API: `POST /api/v1/tasks?start=true`). Validation errors come back as `422` with one message per problem.

## Task JSON reference

The full shape accepted by `POST /api/v1/tasks`, `PUT /api/v1/tasks/{id}`, import and the tasks file. Defaults are applied when a field is empty or zero.

```json
{
  "id": "products",
  "name": "Postgres products",
  "description": "Catalog search",
  "tags": ["shop"],
  "desiredState": "running",
  "source": {
    "connectorId": "pg-main",
    "type": "postgres",
    "dsn": "postgres://cdc:secret@db:5432/shop",
    "database": "",
    "schema": "public",
    "table": "products",
    "slot": "",
    "publication": "",
    "serverId": 0,
    "region": "", "endpoint": "", "accessKeyId": "", "secretAccessKey": "",
    "brokers": [], "groupId": "",
    "driver": "", "cursorColumn": "", "pollInterval": "2s",
    "webhookSecret": ""
  },
  "mapping": {
    "primaryKey": ["id"],
    "primaryKeyField": "id",
    "keepKeyColumns": false,
    "include": [], "exclude": ["internal_notes"],
    "rename": {"customer_email": "email"},
    "softDeleteColumn": "deleted_at", "softDeleteValue": "",
    "geo": {"lat": "lat", "lng": "lng"},
    "timeFormat": "unix",
    "static": {"tenant": "acme"}
  },
  "index": {
    "uid": "products",
    "destinationId": "",
    "writeMode": "replace",
    "manageSettings": true,
    "settings": {"filterableAttributes": ["category"], "sortableAttributes": ["price"]}
  },
  "sync": {
    "mode": "snapshot_stream",
    "batchSize": 1000, "flushInterval": "1s", "maxInflight": 4,
    "retry": {"maxAttempts": 8, "initialBackoff": "200ms", "maxBackoff": "30s"},
    "safety": {
      "maxDeleteRatio": 0.2, "minDocsForDeleteGuard": 1000,
      "allowTruncate": false, "zeroDowntimeResync": true, "dumpBeforeResync": false
    }
  }
}
```

- Use `connectorId` or the inline connection fields (`type`, `dsn`, …), not both: with a connector, the connector's connection fields are used and `type` is taken from it.

- Durations are strings (`"500ms"`, `"2s"`); a plain number is read as milliseconds.

- `desiredState` is `running`, `stopped` or `paused`; the API sets it through actions, the tasks file through this field.

- Responses add `createdAt`, `updatedAt` and a `status` object, and mask secrets as `••••••`. Sending a masked value back keeps the stored secret.


---

URL: https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/task-operations.html

# Operate tasks

Every task has a live state, a set of lifecycle actions and a detail page with its counters, logs and data-quality tools.

The task list: search, filter by source, state or tag, and select several tasks for batch actions.

## States

| State | Meaning |

| stopped | Not running. The checkpoint is kept. |

| starting | Connecting to the source, preparing the index and applying managed settings. |

| snapshotting | Copying existing rows, with progress (done / total; the total is an estimate from the source). |

| resyncing | A snapshot requested by Resync or by a lost source position. |

| streaming | Applying changes in near real time. |

| retrying | The pipeline failed with a transient error and restarts after a backoff (1 s, doubling up to 1 minute; the status shows the attempt and the wait). The backoff starts over after two minutes of healthy running. |

| paused | Stopped by Pause. Like stopped, but kept paused across service restarts. |

| held | A safety guard stopped the task before a mass delete or a truncate. It needs an operator. |

| failed | A configuration error retrying cannot fix (bad credentials, missing table, wrong server settings, primary key mismatch). Fix it, then start again. |

| completed | A snapshot-mode task finished its copy. |

When the service starts, tasks whose desired state is running start again from their checkpoints; paused tasks stay paused.

## Actions

| Action | Role | What it does |

| Start / Resume | moderator | Runs the task from its checkpoint (a snapshot first if it never finished one). |

| Stop | moderator | Drains pending batches (up to CDC_STOP_TIMEOUT) and stops. Unconfirmed changes are replayed on the next start. |

| Pause | moderator | Like stop, but the state is paused. |

| Restart | moderator | Stop, then start. |

| Resync | moderator | Rebuilds the index from a fresh snapshot, then streams from the position captured before it. With zero-downtime resync the copy goes into a shadow index (__cdc_shadow_) created with the live index's settings, which is swapped in when complete; search keeps using the old index meanwhile. Without it, the index is emptied first (in-place resync: clearing …) and fills up again. Refused for tasks in stream mode. |

| Reset checkpoint | moderator | Forgets the sync progress; the next start runs a full snapshot. A running task restarts at once. Documents are not deleted first (unless zero-downtime resync rebuilds into a shadow index), so documents of rows deleted meanwhile can remain; prefer Resync to rebuild. |

| Edit | admin | See Editing a task. |

| Delete | admin | See Deleting a task. |

Actions are available on the task page, in the task list, to the API (`POST /api/v1/tasks/{id}/{action}` with `start`, `stop`, `pause`, `resume`, `restart`, `resync` or `reset-checkpoint`) and to AI agents over [MCP](https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/mcp.html).

### Automatic resync

When the source can no longer resume from the stored position (purged binlog, dropped or invalidated replication slot, expired DynamoDB shard, oplog rolled over, trimmed Redis stream, SQL Server cleanup), the task logs `source position lost (…); starting a full resync` and resyncs by itself, honouring zero-downtime resync.

## Editing a task

Edit opens the wizard with the current definition (admin). Masked secrets are kept unless you replace them.

- A running task restarts with the new definition.

- Changing the source (type, connector, table, schema or database) or the index (uid or destination) clears the checkpoint: the next start runs a full snapshot (`source or index changed: checkpoint cleared, the next start runs a full snapshot`).

- Changing managed settings of a stopped task applies them to the index right away; a running task applies them when it restarts.

- The id cannot change.

## Deleting a task

Deleting removes the definition, checkpoint, status, dead letters and diff report, and stops the task. The confirmation asks you to type the task id and offers two options:

- Drop source replication objects (checked by default; API `dropSource=true`): for PostgreSQL, drops the replication slot and the generated publication, so the database stops retaining WAL. Other sources keep nothing on the server that needs dropping; a Kafka consumer group is left in place.

- Also delete index (API `deleteIndex=`, which must equal the task's index uid): deletes the Meilisearch index and its documents. Otherwise documents stay.

## Batch actions

Select tasks in the list to start, stop, pause, resume, restart, resync or delete them together (moderator; delete needs admin). Up to 8 tasks are processed in parallel and the result of each is reported. A batch delete never drops source objects nor deletes indexes. API: `POST /api/v1/tasks/batch` with `{"ids": [...], "action": "resync"}`.

## Import and export

- Export (admin) downloads every task definition as JSON, with passwords and secret keys masked.

- Import (admin) creates the tasks of a JSON array, stopped. Tasks whose id exists, or that fail validation, are reported and skipped. Replace masked secrets, or use connectors, before importing into another installation.

For tasks kept in Git, use the [declarative tasks file](https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/declarative-tasks.html) instead.

## The task page

A task page: counters, documents per second and lag over time, checkpoint and runtime details.

| Tab | Contents |

| Overview | Counters (upserted, deleted, events, batches, errors, retries, dead letters, coalesced), rate and lag charts over the last ten minutes, snapshot progress, the checkpoint, in-flight batches, the last error. Webhook tasks also show the push endpoint. |

| Logs | The task's activity log (the last 1,000 entries, kept in memory), streamed live with auto-scroll. |

| Schema check | Source columns versus index fields and settings. See Data quality. |

| Diff | Document-level comparison with repair. See Diff and repair. |

| DLQ | Dead letters with replay and discard. See Dead letter queue. |

| Index settings | Desired versus live settings, drift and Apply. See Drift. |

| Config | The task definition as JSON (secrets masked), with links to edit it. |

### Lag and rate

- Lag is the time between a change's commit in the source and its confirmation in Meilisearch. When a streaming task is idle, its lag returns to zero.

- Rate is documents per second, smoothed.

- Last sync is when Meilisearch last confirmed a batch of the task.


---

URL: https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/indexes.html

# Index management

meilisearch-cdc manages the Meilisearch side too: index settings with drift detection, primary keys, swaps, compaction, a search playground and a documents browser, for every destination.

Indexes grouped per instance, with the tasks that write to each.

## The Indexes page

All instances are queried in parallel and their indexes listed per instance (default first). An unreachable instance is shown with its error. Each index shows its primary key, document count, whether it is indexing, and the tasks that write to it. Actions (admin):

- Create index with a uid and an optional primary key. Usually unnecessary: tasks create their index on first write.

- Swap indexes: exchange the contents of two indexes atomically, or rename one to a new uid.

- Compact: ask Meilisearch to compact the index's storage.

- Delete: type the uid to confirm. Refused with `409` while a running task writes to the index; stop the task first.

## An index's page

Open an index for three tabs:

### Search

A playground for Meilisearch searches: query, filter expression, sort (`field:asc` or `field:desc`, comma separated), result limit, and the raw JSON response. Use it to check that a change in the source reached the index, or to try filters before building them into your application.

The search playground.

### Documents

Browse documents page by page and open any document as JSON.

### Settings

The live settings in the settings editor. Changes are previewed (which keys change, from what to what) before they are applied; applying waits up to 30 seconds for Meilisearch and shows its error when it rejects the update. Reset restores Meilisearch's defaults. The primary key of an index can be changed here only while it holds no documents (`409` otherwise).

## The settings editor

The same editor is used in the task wizard (desired settings) and on index pages (live settings). It has a form view and a JSON view. Only the keys you set are sent; unset keys keep Meilisearch's defaults. Sections:

The settings editor; a dot marks sections changed from the defaults.

| Section | Settings | What they do |

| Attributes | searchableAttributes, displayedAttributes, filterableAttributes, sortableAttributes, distinctAttribute | Which fields are searched (in priority order), returned, usable in filters, usable for sorting, and deduplicated. Filterable attributes can use Meilisearch's granular form (attribute patterns with per-pattern features such as facet search or equality-only filters). Field names discovered from the source are offered as suggestions. |

| Ranking rules | rankingRules | The order of relevancy criteria (words, typo, proximity, attribute, sort, exactness) and custom rules such as price:asc. |

| Typo tolerance | typoTolerance | On or off, minimum word sizes for one and two typos, and words, attributes and numbers where typos are not allowed. |

| Synonyms | synonyms | Words that should match each other. |

| Words & tokens | stopWords, dictionary, separatorTokens, nonSeparatorTokens | Ignored words, custom dictionary entries and how text is split into words. |

| Facets, pagination & search | faceting, pagination, proximityPrecision, searchCutoffMs, prefixSearch, facetSearch | Maximum values per facet and facet sorting, the maximum total hits, word-proximity precision, a search time limit, prefix search and facet search. |

| Localized attributes | localizedAttributes | Force the languages used to tokenize some fields. |

| Embedders | embedders | Vector embedders for semantic and hybrid search (source, model or user-provided dimensions, document template, binary quantization…). |

Desired settings in a task are validated when the task is saved: unknown keys are rejected so a typo cannot silently do nothing.

## Managed settings and drift

With Manage index settings on, a task owns the settings it declares:

- When the task starts, the live settings are compared with the desired ones and only the differences are applied (`applying 3 changed index settings` in the log).

- The task's Index settings tab shows desired versus live values, highlights drift (someone changed the index by hand, or a deployment changed the task), and applies the desired settings with one click.

- Only keys present in the desired settings are compared, so settings the task does not manage never show up as drift. Lists whose order does not matter (filterable and sortable attributes, for example) are compared as sets.

- If Meilisearch rejects the update when the task starts, the start fails with Meilisearch's message (`apply settings: …`) and the task keeps retrying with backoff until the settings are fixed. Desired settings that cannot be parsed fail the task outright.

## Primary key guard

When a task starts, it makes sure its index uses the task's primary key field:

- A missing index is created with that primary key.

- An empty index with another primary key is switched to it.

- An index that has documents and another primary key is refused, and the task fails: `index "products" uses "sku" but the task writes "id" and the index holds 1200 documents; use a new index, change mapping.primaryKeyField, or resync with zero-downtime enabled`. A zero-downtime resync builds a fresh shadow index with the new key and swaps it in.

## Instance-level tools

The task queue, dumps, snapshots and experimental features belong to a whole Meilisearch instance and live on the destination's page; see [per-instance pages](https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/destinations.html#instance-pages). The top-level Meilisearch tasks page shows the task queue of every instance.

The Meilisearch task queue, per instance.


---

URL: https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/data-quality.html

# Data quality

Three tools tell you whether an index really matches its source: the schema check, the document diff (with repair), and the dead letter queue of documents Meilisearch refused.

## Schema check

The Schema check tab of a task (any role) compares three things: the source's columns, the fields actually present in the index (with their coverage, the share of documents that have the field), and the index settings. Each field shows where it comes from, its source type, whether it is in the source and in the index, and which settings reference it (searchable, displayed, filterable, sortable, distinct, ranking).

The schema check with issues sorted by severity.

Issues it reports:

| Level | Issue |

| error | index primary key is "sku" but the task writes "id" |

| error | the source has no primary key; set mapping.primaryKey |

| error | settings reference filterable but no document can contain it (a setting names a field the mapping never produces) |

| warning | field exists in the index but not in the source (dropped or renamed column?); a zero-downtime resync removes it |

| warning | date stored as RFC3339 text cannot be range filtered or sorted chronologically; set mapping.timeFormat to unix |

| warning | some documents miss the primary key field |

| info | column is mapped but no indexed document has it yet |

| info | binary column is indexed as base64 text; consider excluding it |

| info | add _geo to filterable/sortable attributes to use geo search |

| info | the index does not exist yet; it is created when the task starts |

## Diff and repair

The Diff tab (moderator to run) compares the source and the index document by document:

- Source pass. Reads every row with the task's own snapshot query, applies the mapping, and keeps a hash of each document.

- Index pass. Pages through every document in the index and compares hashes.

- Detail pass. Re-reads the source for sample documents to show which fields differ, and for repairs.

The report counts documents in the source and the index and the missing (in the source, not in the index), extra (in the index, not in the source) and mismatched (different content) ones, with up to 50 sample ids per category (`sampleLimit`) and, for mismatches, the differing fields with both values. Floats are compared to 15 significant digits, because Meilisearch does not keep the last digit of some floats; without this, documents that are in sync would never compare equal.

A diff runs in the background (at most one per task, for at most two hours) and the report is kept until the next run. It reads the whole table, so schedule large diffs outside peak hours. Memory grows with the number of documents (one hash per document).

### Repair

Repair runs the diff again and fixes the index while it goes, for the categories you choose: re-send missing and mismatched documents, and delete extra ones. Deleting extras is off by default: check the sample ids first, in case another task writes to the same index. Documents Meilisearch rejects during a repair go to the dead letter queue. The log records `repair: 12 upserted, 3 deleted, 0 rejected`.

```bash
# API: run a diff, then read the report
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"sampleLimit": 50, "compareFields": true}' "$CDC/api/v1/tasks/products/diff"
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$CDC/api/v1/tasks/products/diff"

# Repair missing and mismatched documents (runs in the background as well)
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"missing": true, "mismatched": true, "extra": false}' "$CDC/api/v1/tasks/products/diff/repair"
```

Diff versus resync

A repair fixes a handful of documents without rebuilding anything. When most of the index is wrong (after a mapping change, say), a zero-downtime Resync is faster and cleaner.

## Dead letter queue

When Meilisearch refuses a batch because of a document's content, the writer splits the batch in halves until it isolates the offending documents. Everything else is applied; the offenders are stored in the task's dead letter queue (DLQ) with the error, the Meilisearch error code and the number of attempts. The pipeline keeps going.

Dead letters with the reason Meilisearch gave.

### Why documents land there

| Operation | Typical cause |

| upsert, replace, delete | Meilisearch rejected the document: an invalid or missing document id, a malformed _geo or GeoJSON field, the per-document field limit, an invalid _vectors value, a malformed payload, or a single document too large for the payload limit. |

| transform | The row could not become a document at all, usually because a primary key column has no value (row has no value for a primary key column "id"). The original row is stored. |

### Replay and discard

- Replay (moderator) sends the selected entries (or all) to Meilisearch again, after you fixed the cause (for example by adjusting index settings or embedders). Entries that succeed leave the queue; the others stay with their attempt count increased. `transform` entries cannot be replayed: fix the source row or the mapping, and the next change of that row is applied normally.

- Discard (moderator) deletes the selected entries (or all).

Dead letters are kept in the state store until replayed, discarded, the task is deleted, or purged with `meilisearch-cdc admin purge dlq`. The `cdc_dlq_total` metric and the `dlq` alert rule tell you when new ones arrive.


---

URL: https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/monitoring.html

# Monitoring and metrics

Watch pipelines live in the dashboard, scrape Prometheus metrics, probe health endpoints and ship structured logs.

## The dashboard

The Overview page shows the tasks by state, the combined throughput (events per second across all tasks), documents written, firing alerts, dead letters, snapshot progress, each Meilisearch destination's health, and a feed of recent activity. Every page updates live; the top bar shows Live while the event stream is connected and reconnects by itself.

The overview page.

## Live events (Server-Sent Events)

The dashboard is fed by `GET /api/v1/events`, a Server-Sent Events stream you can also consume yourself. It needs authentication; because `EventSource` cannot set headers, this endpoint also accepts the admin token as `?token=`.

| Event | Data | When |

| status | A task status (state, counters, lag, rate, checkpoint…) | On every change, at most about twice per second per task; one per task when the stream opens. |

| log | A task log entry {"time","taskId","level","message"} | As it happens. |

| task | {"id","action"} with created, updated, deleted or diff | When the task list changes or a diff finishes. |

| overview | The same object as GET /api/v1/overview | When the stream opens, then every 2 seconds. |

| destination.health | {"id","health"} | After each destination health check. |

| alert | An alert event | When an alert fires, repeats or resolves. |

```bash
curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $CDC_ADMIN_TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/events
# retry: 3000
#
# event: overview
# data: {"tasks":{"total":3,"byState":{"streaming":3}}, ...}
```

Behind a reverse proxy, disable response buffering for this path; see [Reverse proxy and TLS](https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/reverse-proxy.html).

## Prometheus metrics

Metrics are served at `/metrics` (not under `/api`) in the Prometheus text format. The endpoint requires authentication: use the static admin token (`CDC_ADMIN_TOKEN`) as a bearer token.

```yaml
# prometheus.yml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: meilisearch-cdc
    metrics_path: /metrics
    authorization:
      type: Bearer
      credentials_file: /etc/prometheus/cdc-admin-token
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["cdc.internal:8080"]
```

| Metric | Type | Labels | Meaning |

| cdc_events_total | counter | task, op (upsert, delete, truncate) | Change events read from sources (snapshot rows count as upserts). |

| cdc_documents_total | counter | task, kind (upserted, deleted) | Documents confirmed by Meilisearch. |

| cdc_batches_total | counter | task | Batches confirmed by Meilisearch. |

| cdc_batch_duration_seconds | histogram | task | Time from enqueueing a batch to its confirmation. Buckets from 10 ms doubling to about 20 s. |

| cdc_errors_total | counter | task | Pipeline failures (each restart and each configuration failure). |

| cdc_retries_total | counter | task | Retried Meilisearch operations. |

| cdc_dlq_total | counter | task | Documents sent to the dead letter queue. |

| cdc_lag_seconds | gauge | task | Delay between the source commit and the Meilisearch confirmation of the last batch. |

| cdc_inflight_batches | gauge | task | Batches enqueued but not yet confirmed. |

| cdc_task_running | gauge | task | 1 while the task's pipeline is active, 0 when it stopped. |

The `task` label is the task id. Series of a deleted task are removed. The standard Go runtime (`go_*`) and process (`process_*`) collectors are included. Counters start at zero when the service starts.

### Example queries

```text
# Documents per second, per task
sum by (task) (rate(cdc_documents_total[5m]))

# Tasks lagging more than a minute
max by (task) (cdc_lag_seconds) > 60

# 95th percentile batch confirmation time
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, task) (rate(cdc_batch_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))

# New dead letters in the last hour
increase(cdc_dlq_total[1h]) > 0
```

## Health endpoints

| Endpoint | Auth | Response |

| GET /healthz | none | ok while the HTTP server runs. Use it for liveness and readiness probes. |

| GET /api/v1/health | none | {"status":"ok","meilisearch":{"status":"available","version":"…","destination":"…"}}; the status is unavailable (with error) when the default destination does not answer within 3 seconds, and unconfigured when there is no destination. |

| GET /api/v1/overview | viewer | Task counts by state, total counters, rate, the default instance and every destination's health, and the registered source types. |

| GET /api/v1/tasks/{id}/metrics | viewer | The task's rate, lag, upserted and deleted counts over about the last ten minutes at 2-second resolution, and its checkpoint. |

## Logs

Service logs go to standard error, as text or JSON (`CDC_LOG_FORMAT`), at the level of `CDC_LOG_LEVEL`. Each task also keeps its last 1,000 activity entries in memory, visible on its Logs tab and in the `log` events. See [Logging](https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/configuration.html#logging).

## Alerts

For notifications instead of dashboards, define [alert rules](https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/alerts.html): task state, lag, dead letters, error bursts, stalled snapshots and Meilisearch down, delivered by email, Telegram or webhook.


---

URL: https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/alerts.html

# Alerts and notifications

Alert rules watch tasks and Meilisearch instances and notify you by email, Telegram or webhook when something needs attention, then again when it is resolved.

Rules, firing alerts and the delivery history.

## Before you create rules

A rule can only be created or enabled when email (SMTP) or a Telegram bot is configured (otherwise `409`: alerts need a notification channel). Every rule needs at least one recipient: an email address, a Telegram chat or a webhook URL. Email recipients need SMTP and Telegram chats need the bot (`422` with the reason). A disabled rule can always be saved. Managing rules needs the admin role; viewing them, the history and active alerts needs viewer.

## Rule conditions

| Type | Fires when | Parameters (defaults) |

| task_state | A task is in one of the chosen states. | states (failed, held; retrying and others can be added) |

| lag | A streaming task's lag exceeds the threshold. | thresholdMs, required (the dashboard asks for seconds) |

| dlq | At least count new dead letters arrived within the window. | count (1), window (5m) |

| errors | At least count pipeline errors happened within the window. | count (1), window (5m) |

| stalled | A task in starting, snapshotting, resyncing or retrying made no progress for the for duration. | for (10m) |

| meili_down | A Meilisearch destination is unhealthy. | destinationIds (empty = every destination) |

### Common fields

| Field | Default | Meaning |

| name | required | Shown in notifications. |

| enabled | | Disabled rules are not evaluated. |

| taskIds | empty = every task | The tasks the rule watches (ignored by meili_down). |

| condition.for | 0 | How long the condition must hold before the alert fires (all types; stalled already includes it). |

| severity | warning | info, warning or critical. |

| cooldown | 30m | While an alert keeps firing, a reminder is sent after each cooldown. At least 1m. |

| notifyResolved | off | Also notify when the condition clears. |

| channels | | emails, telegramChatIds, webhookUrl, webhookSecret. |

Rules are evaluated every `CDC_ALERT_INTERVAL` (5 seconds by default), separately for each task (or destination). Alert state is persisted, so a restart does not send the same notification again. Changing a rule restarts its state.

```json
{
  "name": "Pipeline failed or held",
  "enabled": true,
  "condition": {"type": "task_state", "states": ["failed", "held"], "for": "1m"},
  "taskIds": [],
  "severity": "critical",
  "channels": {
    "emails": ["ops@example.com"],
    "telegramChatIds": ["-1001234567890"],
    "webhookUrl": "https://hooks.example.com/cdc",
    "webhookSecret": "whsec_…"
  },
  "cooldown": "30m",
  "notifyResolved": true
}
```

### Test, history and active alerts

- Send test on a rule delivers a test notification (marked `TEST`) on each of its channels and shows each delivery's result. Test notifications are not stored.

- The history lists every firing, reminder and resolution with each delivery (channel, target, success or error), filterable by rule and state.

- Active alerts are the ones firing now; they also appear live in the dashboard.

## Email (SMTP)

Configure it in Settings → Email (admin). Email is also used for invitations and password resets.

SMTP settings with a test email.

| Field | Meaning |

| Host, port | The SMTP server. Port 465 for TLS, 587 for STARTTLS, 25 for a local relay. An empty host disables email. |

| Encryption | auto (default): TLS from the first byte on port 465, STARTTLS otherwise, and plain text only when the server lacks STARTTLS and no password is sent. tls: TLS from the first byte. starttls: upgrade a plain connection. none: plain text, for local relays only. |

| Username, password | Optional. The password is stored encrypted and shown masked. |

| From | The sender address, for example Meili CDC . |

| Public URL | The dashboard URL used in links (overrides CDC_PUBLIC_URL). |

A mode that cannot work on its port is corrected when sending: `starttls` on port 465 uses TLS, and `tls` on ports 25 or 587 uses STARTTLS. If a password would be sent over a server without STARTTLS, sending fails rather than leaking it. Send test email reports the server's answer; typical errors explain the port and mode mismatch, for example the server sent no greeting: it probably expects TLS from the start; use port 465 with TLS, or check the port.

## Telegram

Configure it in Settings → Telegram (admin):

- In Telegram, talk to @BotFather and send `/newbot`. Copy the token it gives you.

- Paste the token and save. The service validates it with the Bot API's `getMe` (an invalid token is refused with `422`) and shows the bot's name. The token is stored encrypted.

- Add the bot to your group, or to your channel as an administrator, then send a message there.

- Find the chat id: open `https://api.telegram.org/bot/getUpdates` and read `chat.id`. Group and channel ids start with `-100`; a public channel can also be addressed as `@channelname`.

- Send a test message from the settings page, then use the id in alert rules.

The API URL defaults to `https://api.telegram.org` and can point to a self-hosted Bot API server. Telegram messages are sent as HTML with a link to the dashboard when a public URL is known; Telegram's flood control (`retry_after`) is honoured.

## Webhook

A rule with a `webhookUrl` POSTs a JSON body to it. The `text` field makes Slack, Mattermost and Discord-compatible endpoints render the alert directly:

```json
{
  "text": "[CRITICAL] Pipeline failed or held · Products\nTask \"Products\" is failed: open source: postgres: connect: …",
  "link": "https://cdc.example.com/#/tasks/products",
  "event": {
    "id": "00000001761500000000-a1b2c3d4",
    "ruleId": "r1", "ruleName": "Pipeline failed or held", "severity": "critical",
    "taskId": "products", "taskName": "Products",
    "state": "firing",
    "message": "Task \"Products\" is failed: open source: postgres: connect: …",
    "at": "2026-10-26T20:12:00Z",
    "deliveries": []
  }
}
```

The subject line in `text` is `[LABEL] rule name · task or destination name`, where the label is the severity in capitals, `RESOLVED` for resolutions and starts with `TEST ·` for test sends. `event` may also carry `destinationId`, `destinationName` and `reminder: true`. `link` is empty when no public URL is known. Delivery is tried up to 3 times within 30 seconds; `429` and `5xx` are retried, other `4xx` responses are not.

### Signed webhook deliveries

Give the rule a signing secret (`channels.webhookSecret`, at least 16 characters; Generate creates a `whsec_…` value, and it requires a webhook URL). Every delivery then carries the same two headers the [webhook source](https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/source-webhook.html#signed-requests) uses:

```text
X-CDC-Timestamp: 1767225600
X-CDC-Signature: sha256=<hex HMAC-SHA256(secret, timestamp + "." + raw body)>
```

The secret is encrypted at rest and returned as `••••••`; send the mask back to keep it. Receivers should recompute the HMAC over the raw body bytes (before any JSON parsing), compare it in constant time, and reject timestamps older than a few minutes to block replays.

#### Verify in Node.js

```javascript
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto';
import express from 'express';

const SECRET = process.env.CDC_ALERT_SECRET;
const app = express();

app.post('/cdc', express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }), (req, res) => {
  const ts = req.get('X-CDC-Timestamp') || '';
  const got = Buffer.from(req.get('X-CDC-Signature') || '');
  const want = Buffer.from('sha256=' + createHmac('sha256', SECRET).update(`${ts}.`).update(req.body).digest('hex'));
  const fresh = Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(ts)) <= 300;
  if (!fresh || got.length !== want.length || !timingSafeEqual(got, want)) return res.sendStatus(401);
  const alert = JSON.parse(req.body);
  console.log(alert.text);
  res.sendStatus(204);
});
app.listen(3000);
```

#### Verify in Python

```python
import hashlib, hmac, os, time
from flask import Flask, request, abort

SECRET = os.environ["CDC_ALERT_SECRET"].encode()
app = Flask(__name__)

@app.post("/cdc")
def cdc_alert():
    ts = request.headers.get("X-CDC-Timestamp", "")
    sig = request.headers.get("X-CDC-Signature", "")
    body = request.get_data()  # raw bytes
    want = "sha256=" + hmac.new(SECRET, ts.encode() + b"." + body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    if not ts.isdigit() or abs(time.time() - int(ts)) > 300 or not hmac.compare_digest(sig, want):
        abort(401)
    print(request.get_json()["text"])
    return "", 204
```

To test a receiver by hand, compute a signature with `openssl` exactly as in the [webhook source example](https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/source-webhook.html#signed-requests).


---

URL: https://meilicdc.javad.dev/guide/security.html

# Team and security

Accounts with three roles, an owner who cannot be locked out, server-side sessions with CSRF protection, brute-force limits, an audit log, and credentials encrypted at rest.

## Roles

| Role | Can |

| viewer | Read everything except users, invitations, SMTP and Telegram settings, MCP settings and tokens, the task export and the audit log. Search indexes and preview settings. |

| moderator | Viewer, plus operate existing tasks: start, stop, pause, resume, restart, resync, reset checkpoint (one or in batch), run diffs and repairs, replay and discard dead letters, test task definitions, push to webhook tasks, cancel Meilisearch tasks, run destination health checks. |

| admin | Everything: create, edit, delete, import and export tasks; connectors and destinations; index changes (create, delete, settings, primary key, swap, compact); dumps, snapshots and experimental features; users and invitations; SMTP and Telegram; alert rules; MCP; the audit log. |

Members, roles and pending invitations.

### Permission matrix

The server enforces a role per API route. Routes not listed below need `viewer` for `GET` and `admin` for everything else, so new routes are locked down by default. The dashboard hides or disables what your role cannot do, and the server answers `403 {"error":"requires role moderator"}` if you try anyway.

| Route | Viewer | Moderator | Admin |

| Any other GET (tasks, logs, metrics, schema check, diff report, DLQ, indexes, settings, documents, connectors, destinations, alert rules and history, overview, /metrics, events) | yes | yes | yes |

| POST /indexes/{uid}/search, POST /indexes/{uid}/settings/preview | yes | yes | yes |

| GET/PATCH /auth/me, POST /auth/me/password | yes | yes | yes |

| POST /tasks/{id}/{action}, POST /tasks/batch (except delete) | no | yes | yes |

| POST /tasks/test (test a task definition) | no | yes | yes |

| POST /tasks/{id}/diff, POST /tasks/{id}/diff/repair | no | yes | yes |

| POST /tasks/{id}/dlq/replay, DELETE /tasks/{id}/dlq | no | yes | yes |

| POST /ingest/{id} (tasks without a signing secret) | no | yes | yes |

| POST /meili/tasks/cancel, POST /destinations/{id}/health/check | no | yes | yes |

| GET /tasks/export, GET /users, GET /invitations, GET /settings/smtp, GET /settings/telegram, GET /settings/mcp, GET /mcp/tokens, GET /audit | no | no | yes |

| Every other POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE (task create, update, delete, import; batch delete; connectors and destinations, including their test endpoints; indexes; dumps; snapshots; experimental features; users; invitations; settings; alert rules; MCP) | no | no | yes |

Connector and destination tests need admin

`docs/api.md` and the dashboard list testing connectors and destinations as a moderator action, but the server's route table does not include `POST /connectors/test`, `/connectors/{id}/test`, `/destinations/test` or `/destinations/{id}/test`, so the default rule applies and they require `admin`; a moderator gets `403`. Moderators can still test a task's connection with Test connection in the task wizard.
